title: Berkshire 2002 letter: float, derivatives as time bombs, and governance reform
summary: Buffett reviews 2002: how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, durability), General Re's reserving and underwriting failures, why he calls derivatives "financial weapons of mass destruction," and why boards, audit committees and CEO pay were broken. Also covers buying to keep, hiring great managers, and refusing to buy stocks at poor prices.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is only valuable if it costs less than other funds; otherwise the insurer is a lemon.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Insurers must underwrite with discipline, reserve conservatively, and avoid dangerous aggregation of risk.
principles.quote: they must: (a) underwrite with unwavering discipline; (b) reserve conservatively; and (c) avoid an aggregation of exposures that would allow a supposedly “impossible” incident to threaten their solvency.

principles.text: Accept lumpy returns if paid appropriately; prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%.
principles.quote: As long as we are paid appropriately, we love taking on short-term volatility that others wish to shed. At Berkshire, we would rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%.

principles.text: Buy good-to-great businesses run by great managers at a sensible price, and buy to keep rather than plan an exit.
principles.quote: Those attributes are two legs of our “entrance” strategy, the third being a sensible purchase price. Unlike LBO operators and private equity firms, we have no “exit” strategy – we buy to keep.

principles.text: Sit out when stocks aren't priced to offer high expected returns; inactivity can be part of good investing.
principles.quote: Unless, however, we see a very high probability of at least 10% pre-tax returns (which translate to 6½-7% after corporate tax), we will sit on the sidelines.
